title_en: Fragments on the Letter to Titus
author: Oecumenius
occasion: Brief exegetical comments on selected verses of Paul's Letter to Titus, preserved in catena form. The fragments address interpretive difficulties raised by the text, especially Paul's use of a pagan poet and his instructions about rebuke and purity.
argument: Oecumenius explains that when Paul quotes the Cretan poet saying 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies,' he does so not to endorse the poet's defense of Zeus's immortality but to affirm the truth of the poet's description of Cretan character. He then comments on Paul's command to rebuke the Cretans sharply, noting that while Paul often teaches gentleness, the Cretans needed the sting of reproof. He further explains that all things are pure to the pure because God made all things pure; but if things are impure, the accusation touches the Creator. He also notes that those who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds are impure, and that Paul's mention of reverent behavior shows women are called to an inheritance. Finally, he treats Paul's instructions about Titus's own conduct, distinguishing incorruptibility of mind and dignity of work, so that one abstains not only from corrupt action but also from corrupt thought.

outline.move: Explains Paul's use of the Cretan poet's saying about Cretans as liars and idle bellies, distinguishing Paul's truthful testimony from the poet's false defense of Zeus.
Comments on why Paul commands sharp rebuke of the Cretans and on the saying that all things are pure to the pure, since God made all things pure.
Notes that those who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds are impure, and explains that Paul's mention of reverent behavior shows women are called to an inheritance.
Distinguishes between incorruptibility of mind and dignity of work, so that one abstains not only from corrupt action but also from corrupt thought.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle and author of the Letter to Titus, quoted and interpreted throughout.

cast.name: Titus
cast.who: Paul's coworker to whom the letter is addressed, mentioned in the title and implied as the recipient of instructions.

cast.name: Cretans
cast.who: The inhabitants of Crete whose character is described as lying and idle.

cast.name: Zeus
cast.who: The Greek god whose tomb on Crete the poet defended, and whose immortality the poet falsely asserted.

cast.name: The poet
cast.who: The pagan poet quoted by Paul, not identified by name in the source; the identification with Epimenides is traditional but not explicit here.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Quoted indirectly through Oecumenius's paraphrase; the lemmata are editorial citations marking the biblical text being commented upon, not direct quotations of Paul's words.

voices.speaker: The poet (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Quoted indirectly through Oecumenius's discussion; the poet's words are embedded in Oecumenius's explanatory paraphrase, not set off as a direct quotation.

key_terms.sense: Liars; the defining vice Paul and the poet attribute to Cretans.
Idle bellies; a vivid image for lazy gluttons.
Testimony or witness; Paul's affirmation that the saying about Cretans is true, contrasted with the poet's false witness to Zeus.
Rebuke sharply; Paul's command to reprove the Cretans with severity because they needed the sting of correction.
Pure; all things are pure to the pure because God made all things pure, so impurity would indict the Creator.
Reverent or befitting a sacred calling; applied to older women, showing they are called to an inheritance.
Incorruptibility or freedom from corruption, applied to the mind.
Dignity or gravity, applied to one's work or conduct.

scripture: The author cites the Letter to Titus by standard New Testament book name and chapter-verse references (e.g., Tit 1,12–13a). No Old Testament or LXX book names appear in these fragments. Modern citations should use 'Titus' with standard chapter and verse numbering.
uncertain: The precise identity of the poet quoted by Paul is not stated in the source; the identification with Epimenides is traditional but not explicit here.
The date of Oecumenius's work is not indicated in the fragments.
The original addressee of the commentary as a whole is not stated in these fragments.

_unresolved_facts.claim: not to endorse the poet's defense of Zeus's immortality
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπιλαμβανόμενος αὐτῶν εἶπεν ὡς κακῶς δεικνύντων τάφον ∆ιὸς τὸν οὐκ ὄντα
_unresolved_facts.fix: not to endorse the poet's false claim about Zeus's tomb (the poet said they showed a tomb of Zeus that did not exist, i.e., the poet accused Cretans of falsely claiming Zeus was dead/had a tomb, not defending Zeus's immortality)

_unresolved_facts.claim: the poet falsely asserted Zeus's immortality
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπιλαμβανόμενος αὐτῶν εἶπεν ὡς κακῶς δεικνύντων τάφον ∆ιὸς τὸν οὐκ ὄντα...ἐκεῖνος ἐψεύσατο τῷ ∆ιῒ συνηγορῶν
_unresolved_facts.fix: the poet falsely asserted that Cretans wrongly showed a tomb of Zeus that did not exist; the poet was 'advocating for Zeus' (συνηγορῶν) by attacking Cretan claims about Zeus's death, not by asserting Zeus's immortality per se

_unresolved_facts.claim: Zeus...whose tomb on Crete the poet defended, and whose immortality the poet falsely asserted
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπιλαμβανόμενος αὐτῶν εἶπεν ὡς κακῶς δεικνύντων τάφον ∆ιὸς τὸν οὐκ ὄντα
_unresolved_facts.fix: Zeus...whom the poet defended by accusing Cretans of falsely claiming there was a tomb for him

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul (quoted)...Quoted indirectly through Oecumenius's paraphrase; the lemmata are editorial citations marking the biblical text being commented upon, not direct quotations of Paul's words
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐχρήσατο δὲ τῷ αὐτῷ στίχῳ Παῦλος...ἐπήγαγεν· ἡ μαρτυρία αὕτη ἀληθής ἐστιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul's words 'ἡ μαρτυρία αὕτη ἀληθής ἐστιν' are directly quoted in the source; this is not merely paraphrase

_unresolved_facts.claim: The poet (quoted)...Quoted indirectly through Oecumenius's discussion; the poet's words are embedded in Oecumenius's explanatory paraphrase, not set off as a direct quotation
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸ Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί
_unresolved_facts.fix: The poet's words appear as a direct quotation in the source, introduced by τὸ and the poet's saying is explicitly quoted

_unresolved_facts.claim: distinguishing incorruptibility of mind and dignity of work
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὸ τῆς ἀδιαφορίας ἐπὶ τοῦ νοῦ ἔλαβεν, τὸ δὲ τῆς σεμνότητος ἐπὶ τοῦ ἔργου
_unresolved_facts.fix: distinguishing ἀδιαφορία (freedom from corruption/integrity) of mind and σεμνότης (dignity/reverence) of work; 'incorruptibility' is not the right rendering of ἀδιαφορία here

_unresolved_facts.claim: Distinguishes between incorruptibility of mind and dignity of work
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὸ τῆς ἀδιαφορίας ἐπὶ τοῦ νοῦ ἔλαβεν, τὸ δὲ τῆς σεμνότητος ἐπὶ τοῦ ἔργου
_unresolved_facts.fix: Distinguishes between ἀδιαφορία (integrity/freedom from corruption) of mind and σεμνότης (dignity) of work
